papers.title: Revealing optimal melting regimes for defect lean single-track aluminium laser powder bed fusion builds
papers.abstract: AlSi10Mg is a typical alloy used in additively manufactured components such as heat exchangers with thin-wall features. However, printing of single-track thin walls remains a challenge owing to inherent process instabilities. Here, we use in situ synchrotron X-ray imaging to develop a process map identifying five distinct melting regimes with their characteristic defect formation tendencies. Quantification of melt pool shape, void formation and melting efficiency, point to an optimal, defect-lean keyhole regime for single track builds with a high melting efficiency of 25% and an energy reduction of ~30% from the commonly used conduction regime. The unstable keyhole region was found to be larger than that reported for other alloys, e.g. Ti-6Al-4V. We also reveal a transitional keyhole flickering phenomenon, causing irregular tracks due to rapid (~1 ms) switching between keyhole and conduction modes, which is explained with the aid numerical simulation and correlated with melt pool size, physical properties and the dimensionless Strouhal number. Process mapping enhances our understanding of processing strategies for thin-wall builds, informing robust, high-quality additive manufacturing methods.

summary_zh.motivation: 研究铝合金单道薄壁打印工艺稳定性，建立缺陷类型图。
summary_zh.method: 利用同步辐射X射线成像结合数值模拟，识别五种熔融模式。
summary_zh.result: 发现最佳缺陷少的小孔熔融模式，熔化效率25%，节能30%。
summary_zh.validation: 通过实验成像和数值模拟验证熔池变化与缺陷形成。

summary_en.motivation: To understand process instabilities in single-track thin-wall AlSi10Mg laser powder bed fusion and identify optimal melting conditions.
summary_en.method: In situ synchrotron X-ray imaging combined with numerical simulation to categorize five distinct melting regimes.
summary_en.result: An optimal defect-lean keyhole regime with 25% melting efficiency and ~30% energy reduction compared to conduction mode is identified.
summary_en.validation: Experimental X-ray imaging and numerical simulations validate the melt pool dynamics and defect formation mechanisms.
